content: 1. Developing skills to manage stress is essential for maintaining mental health in the workplace. 2. Individual interventions, such as manager training for mental health, are effective in promoting and protecting mental health at work. 3. Manager training enhances knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors related to mental health, encouraging workers to seek help when needed. 4. Managers and supervisors, including executive leaders, should undergo mental health training to better support their teams. 5. The purpose of this training is not to turn managers into mental health care providers; they are not expected to diagnose or treat mental disorders. 6. Instead, managers should learn to recognize when and how to direct employees to appropriate support resources and advocate for mental health initiatives in the workplace. 7. Mental health training for managers can be integrated into pre-job training, such as management programs, leadership curricula, or onboarding, as well as on-the-job training. 8. This training can be delivered in various formats, including electronic or face-to-face, guided or self-directed, and individually or in groups, depending on what suits the workforce best. 9. Training should be adapted to local contexts, periodically refreshed, and offered during regular paid working hours. 10. 11. Individual workplace interventions are designed to directly support workers, either with or without guidance from a qualified practitioner. 12. 13. Psychosocial interventions, such as psychoeducation, stress management training (including relaxation and mindfulness), and emotional or practical social support, help reduce mental health symptoms and improve work performance. 14. Evidence shows that these interventions promote positive mental health, reduce emotional distress, and enhance workplace effectiveness. 15. Stress management interventions, including digital self-help tools, are popular among employers due to their ease of delivery, provided resources are available. 16. However, these tools should be part of a broader program that includes preventive and supportive mental health activities, as focusing solely on individual stress management may be ineffective and could wrongly place blame on individuals for workplace stress. 17. Employers must verify the quality and effectiveness of interventions by consulting experts before implementation. 18. While many digital mental health applications exist, only a few have been rigorously tested and evaluated. 19. Workers with mental health conditions should have access to evidence-based psychological treatments, such as behavioral activation, problem-solving therapy, cognitive behavioral therapy, or interpersonal therapy, preferably outside the workplace. 20. Training workers in mental health literacy and awareness improves their knowledge and attitudes, including reducing stigma, and empowers them to value their well-being and seek help when needed. 21. Such training can also encourage help-seeking behavior and should be delivered by competent trainers during regular paid working hours. 22. Involving individuals with lived experience of mental health conditions as co-facilitators can be particularly effective in reducing stigma. 23. People living with mental health conditions have a right to work, and governments and employers must support this right through person-centered, recovery-oriented strategies. 24. The WHO recommends three evidence-based workplace interventions to support individuals with mental health conditions: reasonable accommodations, return-to-work programs, and supported employment initiatives. 25. These interventions promote inclusivity and help individuals with mental health conditions reach their full potential. 26. Supported employment initiatives focus on quickly integrating individuals into paid work while providing ongoing mental health and vocational support. 27. Reasonable accommodations adapt the work environment to meet the needs of individual workers, such as flexible hours, additional time for tasks, or time off for mental health care. 28. Accommodations may also include access to private spaces for rest or medication storage and regular supportive meetings with supervisors. 29. Return-to-work programs help workers re-enter and remain in employment after an absence due to mental health conditions, combining workplace accommodations with evidence-based clinical care. 30. 31. Governments play a critical role in enabling workplace mental health interventions by aligning employment laws with international human rights standards and ensuring non-discrimination. 32. Employers must comply with rights-based laws, implement non-discriminatory recruitment and employment practices, and collaborate with stakeholders to address workers' mental health and vocational needs. 33. 34. 35. Governments and employers should integrate mental health into occupational safety and health (OSH) management systems and national OSH strategies. 36. A comprehensive program of interventions targeting organizations, managers, and workers should be based on evidence about workplace psychosocial risks and the effectiveness of interventions. 37. 38. Regulatory processes should guide employers in implementing interventions and holding them accountable for non-compliance. 39. 40. Stakeholders, including civil society, healthcare providers, and organizations of individuals with lived experience, play a vital role in advocating for and implementing workplace mental health initiatives. 41. 42. Employers’ and workers’ organizations are key partners in designing and implementing workplace mental health policies, raising awareness, and supporting the implementation of OSH regulations. 43. Cooperation between management and workers is essential in addressing workplace mental health issues effectively. 44. All stakeholders in the world of work, including governments, employers, workers, and civil society, must take action to improve mental health at work.
